etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English net, from Old English net, nett, from Proto-West Germanic *nati, from Proto-Germanic *natją, from Proto-Indo-European *ned- (“to turn, twist, knot”).

Cognate with West Frisian net, Low German Nett, Dutch net, German Netz, Danish net, Swedish nät.

definitions.definition: A mesh of string, cord or rope.
A device made from such mesh, used for catching fish, butterflies, etc.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Then there came a reg'lar terror of a sou'wester same as you don't get one summer in a thousand, and blowed the shanty flat and ripped about half of the weir poles out of the sand. We spent consider'ble money getting 'em reset, and then a swordfish got into the pound and tore the nets all to slathers, right in the middle of the squiteague season.

definitions.definition: A device made from such mesh, generally used for trapping something.

quote.citation: 1983, Richard Ellis, The Book of Sharks, Knopf, →ISBN, page 190:
quote.text: The nets have to be checked to make sure that they are not tangled up and therefore useless, and the carcasses of the dead sharks are removed.

definitions.definition: Anything that has the appearance of such a device.
(by extension) A trap.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Proverbs xxix:5:
quote.text: A man that flattereth his neighbor spreadeth a net for his feet.

definitions.definition: (geometry) Any set of polygons joined edge to edge that, when folded along the edges between adjoining polygons so that the outer edges touch, form a given polyhedron.
(electronics) A conductor that interconnects two or more component terminals.
A system that interconnects a number of users, locations etc. allowing transport or communication between them.
(sports) A framework backed by a mesh, serving as the goal in hockey, soccer, lacrosse, etc.

quote.citation: 2010 December 29, Mark Vesty, “Wigan 2-2 Arsenal”, in BBC:
quote.text: Wigan had N'Zogbia sent off late on but Squillaci headed into his own net to give the home side a deserved point.

definitions.definition: (sports, tennis) A mesh stretched to divide the court in tennis, badminton, volleyball, etc.
(tennis, by extension) The area of the court close to the net (mesh stretched to divide the court).
(transitive) To catch by means of a net.
(transitive, figuratively) To catch in a trap, or by stratagem.

quote.citation: 1814 July 7, [Walter Scott], Waverley; or, ’Tis Sixty Years Since. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), Edinburgh:  […] James Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Co.; London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, →OCLC:
quote.text: And now I am here, netted and in the toils.

definitions.definition: To enclose or cover with a net.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto II:
quote.text: Old Yew, which graspest at the stones⁠That name the under-lying dead,⁠Thy fibres net the dreamless head,Thy roots are wrapt about the bones.

definitions.definition: (transitive, soccer) To score (a goal).

quote.text: Romeu then scored a penalty, Torres netted a header and Moses added the sixth from substitute Oscar's cross.

definitions.definition: (tennis) To hit the ball into the net.

quote.citation: 2011 June 28, David Ornstein, “Wimbledon 2011: Victoria Azarenka beats Tamira Paszek in quarters”, in BBC Sport‎[4]:
quote.text: Azarenka whipped a sensational forehand around the net post to break for 2-0 in the second set, followed it up with a love hold and moved to 5-1 when Paszek netted a forehand.

definitions.definition: To form a netting or network; to knit.

quote.citation: 1849 May – 1850 November, Charles Dickens, The Personal History of David Copperfield, London: Bradbury & Evans, […], published 1850, →OCLC:
quote.text: I was shown into a pretty but rather close drawing-room, and there sat Agnes, netting a purse.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English net, nette, from Old French net, from Latin nitidus. Doublet of neat and nitid.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Good, desirable; clean, decent, clear.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto XII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: Her brest all naked, as net iuory, / Without adorne of gold or siluer bright  […]

definitions.definition: Free from extraneous substances; pure; unadulterated; neat.
Remaining after expenses or deductions.
Final; end.
After expenses or deductions.
The amount remaining after expenses are deducted; profit.
(transitive) To receive as profit.
(transitive) To yield as profit for.
To fully hedge a position.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Middle French nettoyer (“to cleanse”).

definitions.definition: (dialectal) To clean, wash, rinse.
